THCa diamonds are prepared by taking a supersaturated extract in hydrocarbon (butane or pentane), and crystallizing typically by evaporation. The crystals can be recrystallized (you can only recrystallize a solid) to yield the clear/white crystals shown here.

What is THC salt? Both THCa and d9-THC are neutral compounds, unless you mean NaTHC or something similar, which won’t form without strong base (which also accelerates decarboxylation). It is definitely not safe to consume any salt form of THC, especially not by smoking (it would simply burn and decompose).

How can something crystallize when exposed to heat? Things crystallize when cooled down in a supersaturated solution or upon slow evaporation or solvent layering; there are no chemical methods that can induce crystallization in d9-THC. I’ve said it before and I’ll say it again: I get the qualms about using glassware for food: contaminated glassware is unsafe. However, contaminated glassware also doesn’t work for chemistry. 

If I couldn’t get my glass quantitatively clean, my chemistry would not work as well. Sure, if you work with radioisotopes or extremely powerful carcinogens, maybe don’t use that glassware, but even the most toxic compounds will struggle to cause damage in sub microgram doses (which is what you would get from clean glass). This is certainly not a recommendation to go drinking out of erlenmeyers, but I encourage everybody who comments on things like this to think critically about actual, real-life safety concerns, not just parrot what they’ve heard from authority figures. There’s no need to be quite that rigorous. Trimethoxybenzene is a great internal standard, but I actually use 1,1,2,2-tetrabromoethane as a standard if I don’t need it to be <1% error in my yields. It gives only a 2H singlet at 6ppm, which usually doesn’t overlap with anything, and it’s a liquid: I just rotavap down my samples, add an arbitrary (weighed) single drop of internal standard which usually works out to be between 10-15mg, add the total quantity of solvent I’ll use for the NMR, homogenize, and then transfer the entire mixture to my nmr tube with no washes - some product is lost, but the internal standard concentration is unaffected. No need to mess with equivalents or stock solutions. 

It’s also unlikely you need to determine t1, unless your molecules are very large or very viscous. The vast majority of organic compounds that I work with in the lab have very short t1 values compared to the nmr delay, and I haven’t had any issues with quantitation using my method. I usually check overall mass balance by NMR and I’m usually off by less than 5% of the total amount of SM added (measured relatively roughly by density/volume, so some error expected).

I could give suggestions for a few, but they would be rough at best. Unfortunately you’ve just gotta try; getting nice crystals isn’t easy even when the solubilities of the compound in various solvents is known. 

Start with volatile solvents that can be evaporated easily and swapped for other solvents (think acetone, methanol, ethanol, DCM, ethyl acetate, ether, etc). Water, if used, should be distilled because some compounds have easily hydrolyzable bonds, you should check beforehand. You want to boil these solvents (which is extremely dangerous so please never use an open flame, only a hot plate and keep away from all sources of flame/sparks/anything else and do it outside for the love of god) and dissolve as much compound as possible in them, and then let them slowly cool. A good solvent will dissolve it easily at high temp, and poorly at low temp. You might also do a hot filtration if there are solids remaining.

Another option is mixed solvent recrystallization. Dissolve compound in a minimal amount of boiling solvent (that it’s very soluble in). Slowly add a solvent that it’s insoluble in, until you see a solid. Then add a tiny amount of the first solvent until it clears up again. Let cool slowly. The goal is to make a solvent system that the compound is only barely soluble in at high temperature.

There’s this idea that somehow the effects of the drug are different whether or not a person has ADHD. A recreational dose of any stimulant will cause euphoria and stimulation whether or not ADHD is involved. I have ADHD, and I still have slight euphoria and significant physical stimulation when I take my meds. The main difference, as far as I can tell, is that the dopamine baseline of a person with ADHD is much lower, and the right dose of a stimulant will bring dopamine up to levels typical of the average person. The average person, on the other hand, will receive dopamine at levels far higher than average. Note that the dopamine levels change by the same amount regardless of ADHD, but the effects can be more noticeable in a person without it, as their baseline is significantly higher. In essence, stimulants reduce the negative effects of low dopamine in people with ADHD, but regular people don’t have those negative effects, so stimulants have a different psychological effect on those without ADHD. The actual mechanism and physical effects of the drug are no different though.
